Photograph: Ronen Tivony/NurPhoto via Getty Images Maryland Two US men charged for allegedly using snakes, a lemur and a monkey for exotic photoshoots Men allegedly used exotic animals for photoshoots featuring a ring of fire in a parking garage in Maryland Edward Helmore Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Baltimore , Maryland, men are facing charges for allegedly using exotic animals – including snakes, a lemur and a spider monkey – in photoshoots featuring three semi-clothed models and a ring of fire in a garage beneath a luxury shopping complex. Photographer Vernon Crowfey III, the 32-year-old owner of the company Photogeniks, was arrested in Towson, Maryland , on 16 July after an undercover officer arranged a shoot with the animals. A second man, Jayden Evans, 25, a collaborator who owns Tarzan Exoticz, which sells personalized photoshoots with exotic animals, was also arrested with Crowfey. The pair allegedly staged a photoshoot in a parking garage beneath Towson Town Center where Crowfey photographed three women posing with the exotic animals. Video footage and photos circulating online show the garage floor lit on fire. Charging documents state Crowfey and Evans obtained the animals from North Carolina without a permit. Evans’s website , Instagram and Facebook pages show photos of him and others with various animals, including “nonhuman primates”. “Vernon Crowfey was observed in a multitude of joint posts with Jayden Evans where he is the photographer for the animal shoots, and Jayden Evans is the animal handler during the photoshoots,” the documents said. The arrests came in a sting operation after a Baltimore police detective confirmed with the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service that neither of the men had a valid Class C exhibitor or dealer license as required under the Animal Welfare Act. An undercover officer later arranged a photoshoot with Evans involving the lemur and spider monkey. A search warrant was executed at Evan’s home, where both men were arrested. Police also found snakes, lizards, rabbits, a tarantula and several other animals at the home. “Based off of what the USDA specialist and Animal Control Officers observed at the scene, neither the lemur or spider monkey were in proper living conditions, which led to their overall neglect,” charging documents said. Both men are each facing 23 misdemeanor and felony charges, including animal cruelty and arson-related offenses, for allegedly setting fire to the mall parking garage. Crowfey claimed to CBS News Baltimore that he was given permission by mall security to use the parking garage as the backdrop for his photoshoot. “We spoke with the security at the mall as well. We explained to him that we was gonna have the fire flame photoshoot. He told us basically just be out before the mall closed,” Crowfey told the network. He also said he wanted to use the space because “we talkin’ about an empty parking lot, with no civilians, full of concrete and I don’t think I’ve ever seen a parking lot be set on fire with lighter fluid.” The lemur and spider monkey were transported to the Maryland Zoo. “Primates are not domesticated. They are wild animals. They have not been in captivity and bred long enough to get that wildlife feature out of them,” Jacob Thompson, owner of Global Pets, told WBAL. “All it takes is for these animals to hit a maturity point or something triggers them to react in a way that’s wild-like.” The arrests come as a new documentary on the exotic wildlife trade, Monsters of God, is released by HBO on Thursday. Film-maker Eric Goode, whose previous hits include pandemic streamer Tiger King, told Vanity Fair last week that pop culture drives demand for exotic and endangered species. “Jurassic Park had this crazy paradoxical effect on pet sales in the US. Finding Nemo made everyone want to buy a clown fish,” Goode said. “When I used to travel in Asia 10 to 15 years ago, I would see owls in the marketplaces, and people would say: ‘Oh, those are Harry Potter birds.’” Explore more on these topics Maryland Baltimore Animals Wildlife US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4547.text: Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has decided that same-sex marriages concluded abroad will not be entered into the country’s official registers. The decision follows requests from couples married in Austria and is based on Slovak law, which defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Prime Minister Robert Fico (SMER-SD) said Slovak legislation does not allow such registrations. However, lawyer János Fiala-Butora argues that European Union law takes precedence and says Slovakia is obliged to respect EU commitments. He added that affected couples can challenge the decision before EU institutions or international courts. The issue follows a European Court of Justice ruling concerning recognition of same-sex marriages within the EU. Source: STVR

https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-how-do-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/4PnBK As AI technology continues to improve, distinguishing between authentic and AI-generated images is becoming increasingly difficult. Image: Mateusz Slodkowski/SOPA Images/IMAGO Advertisement Anyone with an internet connection and access to an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can create photorealistic images within seconds, for free or for very little money, and then spread them on social networks at breakneck speed. The tools used to create AI-generated images are improving rapidly, reducing the number of obvious AI errors – often referred to as AI hallucinations – and making it increasingly difficult for users to determine whether a viral image depicts a real event. Gone are the days when AI tools routinely produced images of public figures with four fingers, an excessive amount of teeth or unnatural body proportions. An additional challenge is that while many images are entirely AI-generated, others are real photos that have been partially altered using AI. This AI-manipulated image of a Hitler look-alike allegedly attending a 2026 World Cup match garnered millions of views on social media Image: X Here's one example: an authentic broadcast image from the 2026 World Cup in which a fan was replaced by an Adolf Hitler lookalike . Of course, the image was actually created using an OpenAI-powered tool. So how can you spot AI-generated images? DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape. Look closely at the picture There a several tell-tale signs that give away that this image was generated with the help of AI, most notably gibberish-filled text Image: X You may remember the story of a Syrian teenager who helped stop a knife attack in the German city of Hamburg in 2025. As the story spread, conflicting accounts of the incident emerged on social media, along with AI-generated images like the one above. The image looks authentic at first glance, but if you zoom in and examine it carefully, you'll find obvious inconsistencies. That's why it's important to take your time and inspect the details. Common AI errors might be hidden in the background, including distorted objects and gibberish-filled text. Putin is supposed to have knelt down in front of Xi Jinping, but a closer looks shows that the picture is fake Image: Twitter/DW If your device doesn't allow you to zoom in far enough, online tools can help. A tool we often use at DW Fact check is Forensically , a free online photo forensics platform that includes a magnifier and other features for examining images closely. Think about the context Remember the Hitler lookalike from above? A supporter resembling the Nazi dictator would almost certainly have attracted immediate attention from broadcasters, stadium officials and other spectators. Fact check: How do I spot AI images? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Yet no reputable media organizations reported such a stir, and no fans in the stadium shared posts showing the lookalike from a different perspective. This example highlights a key verification technique: move beyond the pixels and ask yourself whether the event itself makes sense. One way of doing that is checking whether the apparent event has been covered by trustworthy news organizations. If an image appears to show a highly unusual or controversial incident, but there is no evidence of it in credible reporting, that should raise a red flag. You can also look at who's posting and sharing the image. If the account often shares AI-generated material or appears to have no connection to the event itself, it's wise to treat the image with caution. Find the image source If you're unsure whether an image is real or generated by AI, try to find its source. One way to do this is by conducting a so-called reverse image search. Instead of searching with keywords, you can upload an image to tools like Google Images or TinEye . These tools can help answer several questions: When was the image first uploaded? On which platforms is the image being shared? What are users saying about it in comments and posts? Have any reputable fact-checkers already verified the image? Of course, some AI-generated images may be brand new and therefore produce few or no results. But manipulated images are often based on older, authentic pictures. In those cases, a reverse search can reveal the original image and provide important context. If you find that an image has already been fact-checked, one way to assess the credibility of the article or video is to see whether the organization is certified by the International Fact Checking Network (IFCN) . The IFCN assesses fact-checkers against a set of professional standards, which include being as fair and transparent as possible, being non-partisan, and committing to open and honest corrections. You can find a list of IFCN-certified outlets here , including DW Fact check. The IFCN should not be confused with the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) , a Russian platform with close ties to the Kremlin. Use AI tools with caution AI detectors can help assess whether an image was created or modified using AI. They search for invisible watermarks and other digital traces associated with AI-generated content. There are a few different types. Tech companies such as Google and OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, have developed systems that identify whether their own AI models were used to create or modify an image. Google's SynthID tool can be accessed here , and here is the link to OpenAI's verification tool. A search using OpenAI, the US-based organization behind ChatGPT, indicates that its tools were used to create the image of the Hitler lookalike Image: Open AI Other tools, such as Image Whisperer , AI or Not , and Hive Moderation, estimate the likelihood that an image was manipulated using AI. And then AI chatbots, such as X's Grok, can provide answers to user questions on whether images are real or fake. In the Hitler lookalike example, OpenAI identified a digital watermark, which confirmed it was manipulated using the AI company's tools. One important word of caution: AI detectors often make mistakes. Their findings should not be treated as definitive proof, but rather as one piece of the verification puzzle. If possible, use more than one tool and cross-check the results to reduce the risk of drawing the wrong conclusions. A viral image of a young girl begging for food in Gaza was wrongly identified by Grok as a photo from Iraq taken in 2014. Image: X When in doubt, don’t share Even after following all these steps, you may still be unsure whether an image is real or AI generated. As AI technology continues to improve, distinguishing between authentic and AI-generated images is becoming increasingly difficult. If you cannot verify an image with confidence, our recommendation is simple: don't share it, especially on social media. Instead, consider warning friends and family members privately that the image's authenticity has not been confirmed and that it should be treated with caution. And if you're still unsure, you can always send the image to us at factchecking@dw.com. We may be able to help verify its authenticity. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – András Baka, a former chief justice of Hungary’s Supreme Court, is due to become the country’s next president after the governing Tisza Party agreed on his nomination. Baka, 73, is expected to be elected to the largely ceremonial position by Parliament on Tuesday. It is another symbolic step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s effort to dismantle former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s bastions of power, a move Magyar says voters endorsed when his party won a landslide victory in the April elections. Receive prophetically relevant Christian news from a biblical worldview — delivered by email. Saturday’s nomination marked a major comeback for Baka. The former judge at the European Court of Human Rights was removed as head of Hungary’s Supreme Court by Orbán’s government in 2011, three years before the end of his mandate. BAKA PRAISED FOR EXPERIENCE However, Tisza lawmakers said Baka has always “attached paramount importance to the principle of the separation of powers, consistently standing up for the rule of law and judicial independence.” “We are convinced that Dr. András Baka’s experience and the professional independence he has demonstrated throughout his career represent a significant asset at a time when we are preparing to jointly lay the foundations for Hungary’s new constitutional order,” they added. Magyar, whose election victory ended Orbán’s 16-year rule, has vowed to restore democratic standards while calling for the resignation of officials appointed or elected by Orbán’s party. Removing former President Tamás Sulyok was a key goal of Magyar, who called him a “puppet” of Orbán. Orbán’s Fidesz party condemned the move and pledged to boycott Tuesday’s presidential vote in Parliament. Sulyok reluctantly signed the constitutional amendment passed by Magyar’s ruling party that ended his own presidency last month. PROTESTS AGAINST AMENDMENT The amendment says the new president will remain in office until a new constitution takes effect, or for a maximum of five years. However, there have been protests against amending the current Constitution, known in Hungary as the Fundamental Law, and against the removal of the previous president, an Orbán ally. Thousands of Sulyok supporters recently gathered outside Budapest’s Sándor Palace, the official residence of the president, as witnessed by Worthy News. Protester Bence Rétvári, parliamentary leader of the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP), condemned the “modification of the Hungarian Fundamental Law,” telling Worthy News: “There is no precedent in Europe like this.” He told Worthy News that “with one sentence, they throw out the president of the republic. It has never happened in the European Union.” SULYOK RESPONDS In a message to the nation, Sulyok shared those concerns but said he had no constitutional means to challenge the move leading to his dismissal. “I have no constitutional means to challenge this amendment, which violates constitutional principles but was adopted by the National Assembly—the body empowered to amend the Constitution—through a lawful procedure,” he stressed. While the role is largely ceremonial, the president can veto legislation and serves as commander in chief of Hungary’s armed forces. Lift this up in Prayer 7 people are currently praying.
